title: Pick a Side? There Are No Sides.
dek: For a long time, finance operated through clearly defined categories.
coverAlt: Weekly Blockchain Digest cover for Pick a Side? There Are No Sides.

content.text: (Published for founders, investors, builders, and curious minds)
For a long time, finance operated through clearly defined categories.
Banks held money. Exchanges traded assets. Payment companies moved money. Crypto companies dealt in tokens. Stock exchanges handled securities.

Last week, SoFi and Kraken connected their banking and crypto infrastructure. Goldman Sachs, Bank of America, Citi and Deutsche Bank joined a 21-institution plan for a dollar stablecoin. Revolut received conditional approval for a U.S. banking charter. The London Stock Exchange partnered with Kraken parent Payward to put U.K. equities on-chain. And Robinhood found itself in a fight with AMC over whether a token tracking its stock is really a share at all.
The underlying shift is bigger than crypto entering traditional finance.
Financial categories are collapsing into each other.
That creates enormous opportunity because products can now combine banking, trading, settlement, payments and tokenization inside the same infrastructure.
But it also creates the next major problem for regulators and markets: when everything starts looking like everything else,
who gets to define what it is?
is one of the computers responsible for deciding which transactions become part of a blockchain’s official record.
Think of a blockchain as a shared financial ledger with thousands of people constantly trying to write new information into it. Someone still has to determine whether a transaction is legitimate.

, validators put economic value at risk, usually by staking tokens, in exchange for the right to verify transactions, create blocks and help secure the network. If enough validators agree that a transaction follows the network’s rules, it becomes part of the blockchain.
That makes validators much more than servers. They are part of the
governance and trust architecture of a decentralized financial system.
This becomes more important as blockchains begin supporting activities traditionally controlled by centralized financial institutions.

If tokenized stocks trade on-chain, stablecoins settle payments, AI agents execute transactions and banks issue assets over blockchain networks, someone still has to determine which transactions are valid.
In traditional finance, that authority sits with banks, exchanges, clearinghouses and settlement institutions. On a public blockchain, part of that responsibility shifts to
. So as financial infrastructure becomes more decentralized, an important question follows:
“We chose the national bank path deliberately.”
Dee Choubey, co-founder and CEO of OpenReserve

, after the OCC granted preliminary approval for its national bank charter. Choubey argued that supervision, compliance and customer confidence are foundations rather than obstacles to building an on-chain bank.
“The financial system should not shut down when markets stay open.”
, explaining why Kraken parent Payward is joining SoFi’s 24/7 dollar settlement network while Kraken lists SoFiUSD and SoFi taps Kraken Prime for crypto liquidity.

, responding after AMC Entertainment CEO Adam Aron demanded that Robinhood stop offering tokens linked to AMC shares. The dispute has become a real-world test of what ownership means when a financial product can replicate a public company’s stock without being issued by that company.
“Your setting up some kind of fictitious synthetic equity market decouples stock token ownership from a company’s ability to control its own capital raising efforts.”
Adam Aron, CEO of AMC Entertainment

, challenging Robinhood’s tokenization model and arguing that synthetic stock products can affect shareholder rights and corporate capital formation even when the underlying company never authorized them.

items.text: The U.S. OCC gave preliminary approval to OpenReserve Bank

, backed by investors including Andreessen Horowitz and Coinbase Ventures. Unlike crypto companies seeking only limited trust charters, OpenReserve chose a full national bank model designed around stablecoin issuance, tokenized deposits and embedded on-chain settlement. The distinction between a “crypto company” and a “bank” becomes much harder to maintain when the institution is legally one and technologically the other.
Revolut also received conditional approval for a U.S. national bank charter.

The company plans to invest roughly $95 million in the operation and expects the bank to offer checking accounts, lending, cards, foreign exchange and eventually a stablecoin. Fintechs are no longer simply competing around the edges of banking; they are acquiring the licenses required to become banks themselves.
The
SEC proposed an overhaul of transfer-agent regulation while beginning work around round-the-clock U.S. securities trading

. Transfer agents maintain official records of who owns securities. That role becomes strategically important when shares are represented as blockchain tokens and markets operate continuously rather than during traditional exchange hours. Tokenization therefore forces regulators to rethink not only the asset, but the market infrastructure surrounding ownership itself.
The legal battle over
prediction markets moved closer to the U.S. Supreme Court
after New Jersey became the first state to ask the Court to resolve conflicting rulings over whether states can restrict products offered by federally regulated platforms such as
Kalshi
. The underlying issue is jurisdiction: new financial products can cross regulatory categories faster than federal and state authority can be cleanly divided.
Meanwhile, the
National Sheriffs’ Association withdrew its opposition to the CLARITY Act and moved to a neutral position

, removing one prominent law-enforcement objection while unresolved questions around DeFi, anti-money-laundering obligations and regulatory jurisdiction remain. The debate has moved beyond whether the U.S. needs crypto market structure rules toward the harder work of deciding exactly where responsibility sits.

content.text: The first regulatory challenge was deciding whether crypto should be allowed inside the financial system. The next one is considerably harder. A company can now be a bank, exchange, stablecoin issuer, brokerage, blockchain operator and payments platform at the same time. An asset can behave like a stock without necessarily being the stock. A prediction contract can look like a federally regulated derivative and a state-regulated wager simultaneously.
Technology is erasing distinctions faster than regulation can redraw them.
The next generation of financial regulation will therefore be less about regulating individual products and more about deciding
which rules follow which economic function.

items.text: A coalition of
21 financial institutions including Goldman Sachs, Bank of America, Citi and Deutsche Bank

announced plans to form a company that could issue a U.S. dollar stablecoin in the first half of 2027, with euro and other G7 currency versions potentially following. A separate 37-member consortium, Qivalis, is developing a euro stablecoin. Stablecoin competition is shifting from crypto-native issuers against banks toward competing banking consortiums designing their own digital money.
The scale gap remains enormous.
Tether has more than $180 billion of USDT outstanding

, while Societe Generale’s dollar stablecoin has only about $12.5 million in circulation. Banks possess distribution, licenses and customer relationships, but those advantages have not yet translated automatically into stablecoin adoption. The battle will be determined by liquidity and usefulness, not simply institutional credibility.
SoFi and Kraken connected both sides of the emerging market.

Kraken parent Payward will use SoFi’s banking services and 24/7 dollar settlement network, Kraken will list SoFiUSD, and SoFi will use Kraken Prime as an additional liquidity source for customer crypto trades. Instead of a bank competing with a crypto exchange, each is becoming infrastructure for the other.
Singapore’s Monetary Authority proposed requiring 100% reserve backing for regulated stablecoins while prohibiting issuers from paying yield.

The framework also creates a path toward recognition of foreign stablecoins and deliberately aligns parts of Singapore’s model with emerging U.S. and European rules. Stablecoin regulation is beginning to converge around the idea that payment tokens should behave like reliable money, not disguised investment products.
A
Bank of Korea study found that demand for dollar-backed stablecoins on Binance was associated with depreciation pressure on local currencies

as market makers rebalanced positions. That adds a monetary-policy dimension to stablecoin adoption: a digital dollar can function as efficient payment infrastructure while simultaneously making it easier for capital to migrate away from weaker domestic currencies.

content.text: Stablecoins began as crypto’s substitute for dollars. They are becoming something much more consequential. Banks want to issue them. Fintechs want to integrate them. Crypto exchanges provide their liquidity. Regulators are designing reserve regimes around them. Central banks are studying their effect on national currencies. Stablecoins are no longer sitting beside the monetary system.
They are starting to become part of the monetary system itself.

items.text: Bitcoin broke back above $81,000 on September 4
, while the broader crypto market rallied alongside equities. Privacy assets led the move, with
Zcash rising roughly 20% and Monero about 8% over 24 hours
. The important signal was not another Bitcoin milestone, but broader participation: capital was moving beyond the largest assets as improving risk appetite spread through the market.
The macro backdrop remained conflicted. Bitcoin had slipped below
$80,000 earlier in the week following Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh’s inflation warning

, before recovering as investors balanced persistent inflation risk against dollar weakness and expectations for monetary policy. Crypto is trading less like an isolated asset class and more like another expression of global liquidity expectations.
Institutional positioning expanded beyond Bitcoin.
U.S. spot XRP ETFs attracted roughly $160 million over nine days

, while Goldman Sachs emerged as the largest disclosed institutional holder. The significance is not XRP outperforming Bitcoin. ETF infrastructure is creating regulated pathways for institutions to allocate across a broader digital-asset universe rather than treating Bitcoin as the industry’s only investable institutional asset.
ARK Invest purchased approximately $37 million of Block shares

on September 1, adding exposure to a company sitting directly at the intersection of payments, Bitcoin and consumer financial services. Public equities are becoming another way institutional portfolios express a view on digital financial infrastructure without holding crypto assets directly.
The broader crypto market reached approximately
$2.82 trillion on September 3

, according to The Block, as digital assets rallied alongside U.S. stocks. The correlation matters. Regulatory clarity, ETF distribution and institutional infrastructure may change crypto’s long-term fundamentals, but short-term capital still responds to the same liquidity, rates and risk appetite driving traditional markets.

content.text: . Bitcoin ETFs opened one door. XRP ETFs, public equities such as Block, institutional custody and regulated bank trading are opening others.
The boundary between a crypto allocation and a traditional financial allocation is becoming harder to identify.
That is exactly the larger story of last week.

items.text: The
London Stock Exchange Group agreed to work with Kraken parent Payward

on bringing major U.K. equities on-chain. LSEG would provide market data and reference pricing while Payward supplies tokenization and trading infrastructure. One of the world’s oldest financial-market institutions is therefore exploring a model in which the economic exposure to traditional securities can travel through blockchain infrastructure.
South Korea set February 2027 as the target for the first phase of a comprehensive tokenized-securities market.

The Financial Services Commission plans a three-stage rollout covering debt and investment-contract securities first, followed by equity-linked products and eventually a broader range of securities. Korea is treating tokenization not as a separate crypto market but as a
new technological layer for its existing capital markets.
Standard Chartered launched institutional Bitcoin and Ether spot trading in the UAE

, becoming the first global systemically important bank to offer the service in the country. The bank is integrating digital assets into the same institutional framework through which clients already access currencies and other financial products. Crypto trading is becoming a banking product rather than something banks merely provide access to through third parties.
Robinhood Chain became one of crypto’s largest fee generators after a memecoin-creation application drove a surge in activity.

Users were creating and trading tokens tied to memes and internet culture, demonstrating how inexpensive token creation can turn attention itself into a programmable financial object. The technology lowers the barrier between cultural expression, community formation and market creation to almost zero.
That same accessibility creates the opposite problem.
AMC Entertainment challenged Robinhood’s stock tokens

, arguing that synthetic products referencing AMC shares were created without the company’s authorization. Blockchain makes assets easier to represent and distribute, but technological ability does not automatically confer legal ownership rights. The next tokenization battle will therefore be as much about the relationship between an on-chain representation and the underlying asset as about the blockchain carrying it.

content.text: Tokenization has reached a more difficult stage. The technical question

The institutional questions are harder: Who authorizes the token? Who maintains the official ownership record? What rights does the holder actually receive? Who settles it? Who regulates it? And what happens when the issuer of the underlying asset never agreed to participate?
Putting finance on-chain does not eliminate intermediaries and rules.
It forces us to decide which ones still matter.

items.text: OpenAI introduced Astra, an AI cybersecurity system capable of discovering previously unknown software vulnerabilities and constructing working exploits with substantially less human intervention.
OpenAI also committed
$1 billion to cyber defense

, explicitly positioning advanced AI as both a growing security threat and a defensive capability. For blockchain systems holding billions of dollars in directly accessible assets, autonomous vulnerability discovery changes the economics of both attacking and defending software.
The concern became more concrete a day earlier when
OpenAI said Astra could construct attacks without human assistance

in controlled evaluations. Smart contracts are particularly exposed to this shift because vulnerabilities can often be monetized immediately: software identifies the weakness, constructs an exploit and potentially interacts directly with an on-chain pool of capital.
AI therefore compresses the distance between discovering a bug and economically exploiting it.
At the consumer layer,
MoonPay integrated crypto transactions into xAI’s Grok

, allowing users to initiate purchases through a conversational interface. The significance is not another chatbot integration. AI is becoming an interface through which users can discover an asset, make a financial decision and execute the transaction without navigating a conventional exchange interface.
The institutional layer is developing in parallel.
Dunamu and Visa
are working on stablecoin infrastructure that includes AI-initiated payments, while
SoFi and Kraken

are connecting always-on banking and crypto settlement. Combine those developments and the architecture begins to look different: AI becomes the decision and interaction layer, stablecoins become the payment layer, and banks, exchanges and blockchains compete to provide settlement underneath.

That architecture also raises a regulatory question that has barely been answered. If an AI agent discovers an investment, borrows against collateral, exchanges currencies and sends a stablecoin payment autonomously, the traditional categories of
customer, adviser, broker, payment initiator and software provider
begin to overlap. AI is therefore accelerating the same category collapse already occurring between banks, exchanges and crypto companies.

content.text: AI is not merely another industry adopting blockchain. It may fundamentally change

Humans historically interacted with banks and exchanges through interfaces designed around human decisions. AI agents can search, compare, decide and execute continuously. That means tomorrow’s financial infrastructure may need to serve two very different types of economic participants:

And both will need identity, permissions, liquidity, settlement, security and regulation. The companies that control those layers may become far more important than the applications sitting on top of them.

items.text: United States:
the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
(OCC) gave preliminary approval to OpenReserve Bank
a blockchain-native institution.

OpenReserve intends to combine a national bank charter with stablecoins, tokenized deposits and on-chain settlement. The U.S. experiment is moving beyond allowing banks to interact with crypto: it is creating a pathway for institutions designed around blockchain to become banks themselves.
United Kingdom:
the
London Stock Exchange Group and Kraken parent Payward

agreed to work together on bringing major U.K. equities on-chain, while Hargreaves Lansdown, Britain’s largest retail investment platform, opened access to crypto ETNs after previously warning clients against cryptocurrency exposure. Two different parts of the traditional investment stack moved toward digital assets in the same week: the market infrastructure itself and the distribution platform connecting it to investors.
South Korea:
the
Financial Services Commission

targeted February 2027 for the first stage of a full tokenized-securities market, beginning with debt and investment-contract securities before expanding toward equity-linked products. At the same time, a
Bank of Korea

study warned that dollar stablecoins can create depreciation pressure on domestic currencies. South Korea is confronting both sides of digital finance simultaneously: tokenization can modernize domestic capital markets, while borderless digital dollars can weaken national monetary control.
Brazil:

Brazilian authorities advanced new rules governing crypto businesses and stablecoins as policymakers confront their growing use in payments and cross-border transactions. Brazil’s significance is practical: stablecoins are not entering a financial vacuum. They are competing with an already sophisticated instant-payment system built around
Pix
, forcing regulators to determine where private digital currencies fit beside successful public payment infrastructure.
Nigeria:
the
Nigerian SEC reported approximately $92 billion in crypto transactions over the preceding year

and moved toward regulating stablecoins and other digital assets under its developing framework. Nigeria’s scale makes the regulatory question different from markets where crypto remains marginal. With substantial existing usage, regulation is less about deciding whether digital assets should exist and more about bringing economic activity already occurring into a supervised financial system.

content.text: The same technology is creating very different policy problems around the world. There will not be one global financial architecture. But the boundaries between
banking, payments, securities and crypto are becoming harder to preserve almost everywhere.

items.text: Cross-chain infrastructure project
TAC
suffered a security incident (~$3.2 million) involving
compromised privileged access

, allowing an attacker to move assets from protocol-controlled infrastructure. The incident demonstrates an important distinction between blockchain security and smart-contract security: decentralized code cannot protect funds if the credentials controlling critical infrastructure are compromised.
KiiChain

suffered an attack involving its blockchain infrastructure that allowed an attacker to exploit weaknesses in the network’s operation and extract assets (approximately $3 million). Layer-1 networks are often treated as the security foundation underneath applications. When the base network itself fails, every application relying on its assumptions inherits the problem.
The
Liquid Network
, Blockstream’s Bitcoin sidechain, paused operations after white-hat researchers identified a vulnerability and moved approximately
$320 million in Bitcoin
as part of the response. The funds were not reported as an attacker loss, making the distinction important: $320 million was exposed or moved during remediation, not stolen.
Hardware-wallet manufacturer
Trezor
disclosed that another approximately
67,000 customers

were affected by a breach involving logistics provider ShipMonk. No direct crypto loss was reported, but customer information connected to hardware-wallet ownership creates a different type of risk: attackers can use identity and shipping information for phishing, impersonation or potentially physical targeting.

content.text: The security perimeter keeps expanding. A validator can work correctly while a private key is compromised. A hardware wallet can remain secure while customer data leaks through a logistics provider. A smart contract can be safe while the blockchain underneath it fails. And now AI systems can autonomously search for vulnerabilities at machine speed.
The future of financial infrastructure therefore depends on more than secure code.
Every dependency becomes part of the security model.
We spent years trying to decide which side would win: crypto or banks. Decentralized finance or traditional finance. Stablecoins or bank deposits. Blockchains or stock exchanges.
That framing is beginning to look wrong. The more interesting outcome is

A crypto company can become a bank. A bank can issue a stablecoin. A stock exchange can use blockchain. A crypto exchange can provide infrastructure to a bank. An AI agent can become the interface connecting all of them. And
once those boundaries disappear, something important happens.
Competition stops being defined by industry. It becomes defined by
And who is responsible when something goes wrong?
The companies that answer those questions best may not look much like today’s banks, exchanges, fintechs or crypto companies. They may be combinations of all four.
The future of finance may not belong to one side or the other. It may belong to the companies that no longer fit neatly on either side and unafraid to trail-blaze the path forward.

title: Plot Twist: the Banks Want In
dek: The regulatory direction is becoming clearer. The response from the financial system is already visible.
coverAlt: Weekly Blockchain Digest cover for Plot Twist: the Banks Want In.

content.text: (Published for founders, investors, builders, and curious minds)
The regulatory direction is becoming clearer. The response from the financial system is already visible.
Thirty-nine U.S. state banking associations announced plans for a

. Swift is building blockchain capabilities into a network connecting 11,500 financial institutions. Japan is designing blockchain settlement for stocks and government bonds. Visa expanded stablecoin infrastructure partnerships in South Korea. The ECB openly argued that central banks themselves need to “go on-chain.”
That changes the competitive landscape. The question is no longer whether blockchain replaces traditional finance.
Banks, payment networks, central banks and crypto companies are now competing to determine
whose infrastructure becomes the place where money actually moves.
Blockchain won the argument that financial rails can be programmable.
The next battle is over who controls them.
refers to a family of open-source blockchain technologies originally developed under the Linux Foundation’s Hyperledger initiative and now housed within
Unlike Bitcoin or Ethereum, Hyperledger was designed primarily for organizations that need distributed ledgers without necessarily making every transaction public.
Think of it as blockchain infrastructure for environments where participants know who they are.

, allows organizations to build permissioned networks where access, privacy and governance can be controlled. The newer Fabric-X architecture is designed for large-scale systems such as digital currencies, stablecoins, tokenized securities and settlement networks.
Hyperledger technologies can be used for:

items.text: Tokenized securities
Banking and settlement networks
Trade finance
Digital identity
Supply chains
CBDC and stablecoin infrastructure

content.text: The financial system being built today will not exist entirely on public blockchains. Banks, governments and market infrastructure providers increasingly want blockchain’s programmability while retaining privacy, governance and regulatory control.

Hyperledger represents one of the architectures built specifically for that middle ground. And that middle ground is becoming strategically important as traditional finance builds its own blockchain rails.
“If anyone can do it, it’s Swift because of the network effect they have.”
Debo Sen, Head of Digital Assets at Citi
, arguing that Swift’s connections to 11,500 financial institutions could allow the existing banking network to become an interoperability layer for blockchain-based finance.
Isabel Schnabel, Member of the Executive Board of the European Central Bank
, arguing that central banks must integrate with blockchain infrastructure to preserve their role in monetary policy, liquidity provision and settlement.
“[Fiscal] debt and deficit levels are a major concern for markets.”
Robbie Mitchnick, Head of Digital Assets at BlackRock
, arguing that persistent concerns around U.S. fiscal policy strengthen the investment case for scarce assets such as Bitcoin and gold.
“It’s an unprecedented collaboration representing thousands of banks.”
Kathy Kraninger, CEO of the Florida Bankers Association and interim chair of the BankChain Alliance
, describing the new nationwide blockchain network backed by 39 U.S. state banking associations.

items.text: Thirty-nine U.S. state banking associations formed the BankChain Alliance
, targeting a 2027 launch of an industry-owned blockchain network for stablecoins, tokenized deposits and programmable payments. The project represents an
important strategic reversal
: banks that spent years challenging crypto policy are now planning blockchain infrastructure inside the regulated banking perimeter.
Britain moved to give the
Bank of England a new statutory objective supporting innovation in stablecoins and digital payments

, while keeping financial stability as its primary mandate. That is a meaningful policy shift because regulators are no longer being asked only to control digital money; they are being instructed to help develop it.
The
European Central Bank

pushed the argument further. Executive Board member Isabel Schnabel said the ECB should embrace blockchain for monetary-policy operations and liquidity provision, warning that failing to integrate with tokenized markets could weaken central banks as private digital money expands. The ECB’s
Pontes and Appia initiatives
are already exploring how central-bank money connects to blockchain settlement.
The
SEC
sent proposed changes to U.S.
crypto custody rules
to the White House for review, extending the regulatory buildout beyond token issuance into the infrastructure that determines who can safely hold digital assets for investors.
Meanwhile, state-level courts complicated the prediction-market model.
Kalshi lost an important ruling affirming Connecticut’s authority to regulate certain prediction-market activity
, reinforcing that federal CFTC oversight does not automatically eliminate state jurisdiction.

content.text: The policy debate is entering a new phase. Governments are no longer simply writing rules around blockchain companies. They are defining how
banks, central banks, exchanges and regulated market infrastructure can build blockchain systems themselves.
The regulators are no longer standing outside the technology. They are becoming architects of it.

items.text: Visa expanded its South Korean stablecoin strategy twice in one week.

Shinhan Financial Group agreed to test stablecoin issuance, remittances, redemptions and AI-powered payments using Visa infrastructure, followed by a partnership with Dunamu, operator of Upbit, to explore stablecoin settlement and purchases initiated by AI agents.
South Korea is becoming a live test market for combining traditional payments, crypto exchanges and autonomous commerce.
SBI Holdings agreed to acquire 20% of Indonesia’s Ajaib Group for $270 million

as part of its plan to distribute the yen-denominated JPYSC stablecoin across Southeast Asia. The investment gives SBI access to a brokerage platform serving one of ASEAN’s largest retail investment markets while creating distribution for blockchain-based cross-border settlement.
Swift’s blockchain strategy became much clearer.
Its existing network processes messaging for
11,500 institutions across more than 200 countries

, facilitating an estimated $1.2 trillion to $1.5 quadrillion of annual payments. Rather than abandoning that distribution, Swift is adding a shared blockchain ledger designed to connect tokenized deposits and fragmented bank networks.
A Dallas Federal Reserve analysis warned that
programmable tokenized deposits could potentially reduce U.S. banks’ ability to support long-duration lending by roughly $700 billion
if money can automatically move between institutions in search of higher yields. The same technology that makes money more efficient can also make deposits less sticky.
The BIS offered the opposite strategic vision from many stablecoin companies. General Manager
Pablo Hernández de Cos
argued that stablecoins are unlikely to become credible payments infrastructure at global scale and that tokenized bank deposits should instead form the core of everyday digital payments.

content.text: The biggest competition in digital money may not be

items.text: Stablecoins versus tokenized deposits.
Private payment networks versus bank-owned ledgers.
Public blockchains versus regulated settlement systems.

content.text: And underneath all of them is the same question:

items.text: Bitcoin broke above
$80,000 on August 25
, reaching its highest level since May. But the more important signal was what moved with it. Gold also strengthened while the U.S. dollar weakened, placing Bitcoin inside the broader
“debasement trade”

rather than a crypto-specific rally. Concerns over U.S. debt, Treasury intervention in long-duration bonds and the purchasing power of fiat currencies were pushing capital toward scarce assets. Bitcoin was up roughly
28% for August
at that point.
The rally also showed how quickly regulatory expectations can become a capital-flow variable. Reuters calculated Bitcoin had risen roughly
16% since President Trump called for clearer crypto legislation

, meaning Washington was being priced alongside interest rates, liquidity and the dollar. Regulation is no longer merely a legal risk for digital assets. It is becoming part of their macro valuation framework.
BlackRock’s
Robbie Mitchnick
argued that
Bitcoin’s long-term macro case is strengthening

as government debt and deficits become larger concerns for markets. That positioning matters because the institutional Bitcoin thesis is moving away from “high-growth technology asset” toward something closer to a portfolio hedge against fiscal and monetary instability.
Traditional brokerage distribution widened at the same time.
Charles Schwab
announced plans to add Solana, Avalanche and Chainlink

to Schwab Crypto after launching direct Bitcoin and Ether trading earlier this year. Crypto exposure is moving deeper into the same accounts where investors already hold stocks, bonds and ETFs, reducing another layer of friction between digital assets and traditional portfolios.
By the end of the week, Bitcoin’s ability to hold around $80,000 was being tested by a familiar force: monetary policy. Markets turned toward Fed Chair
Kevin Warsh’s Jackson Hole remarks

, with inflation expectations and the future path of rates again influencing positioning. Crypto may now have clearer regulation and broader institutional access, but the cost of capital still sets the gravitational field around every risk asset.

content.text: Bitcoin is becoming more integrated into macro portfolios at precisely the moment blockchain is becoming more integrated into financial infrastructure. Those are different trends, but they reinforce each other.
The asset is being evaluated against
, while the technology underneath the industry is being evaluated against
Swift, securities settlement and banking infrastructure
Crypto is becoming less economically isolated from the financial system it was originally built outside of.

items.text: Coinbase launched tokenized versions of Apple, Nvidia, Meta and Alphabet shares on Base

, initially under its Abu Dhabi regulatory framework. This moves Base beyond crypto-native assets and into the infrastructure layer beneath traditional securities. The bigger race is no longer simply which exchange lists the most assets. It is whether exchanges and blockchains can eventually compete with brokers, clearinghouses and settlement networks for the same financial activity.
South Korea’s
POSCO International
, a roughly $22 billion trading company, worked with
Olea and Intain
to tokenize trade receivables on
Avalanche
. Receivables are particularly important because they connect blockchain to working capital rather than speculation.
Tokenization
can turn an otherwise illiquid corporate claim into an
asset that is easier to finance, transfer and potentially distribute to investors.
Bitfinex Securities raised $50 million
as it prepares a tokenized security linked to a Luxembourg industrial-metals platform holding approximately
$1.6 billion of high-purity nickel wire

. Tokenization is moving from Treasuries and funds toward physical commodities and industrial assets, testing whether blockchain can become infrastructure for markets that historically suffered from fragmented ownership records and limited liquidity.
India disclosed plans for its first tokenized corporate bond pilot.
State-owned
REC
is expected to issue less than ₹5 billion, approximately
$57 million
, with settlement using India’s wholesale CBDC. Investors would use one wallet for digital rupees and another for tokenized securities. That architecture is worth watching because it combines
central-bank money and blockchain securities into the same settlement process
, potentially eliminating parts of the reconciliation layer between cash and assets.
Malaysia moved in parallel.
CIMB completed a $342.7 million tokenized sukuk pilot

, part of a larger Islamic bond issuance, while working with the Securities Commission Malaysia on tokenized capital-market products. Tokenization is therefore spreading across very different financial structures, from U.S. equities to Korean receivables, industrial nickel, Indian bonds and Islamic finance.

content.text: The most important blockchain story this week was not another faster chain. It was the diversity of assets moving onto the rails.
Stocks. Trade receivables. Commodities. Corporate bonds. Sukuk.

That is what financial infrastructure adoption actually looks like: not one dramatic migration, but individual asset classes gradually becoming programmable. And that brings us back to the week’s central question.
If more of the world’s assets become tokenized,
which network ultimately becomes the ledger they live on?

items.text: MoonPay integrated Kamino into PayBox

, allowing eligible users to lend assets or borrow against crypto collateral on Solana through conversations with ChatGPT or Claude. Users can approve transactions individually or authorize an AI agent to operate within predefined limits. Kamino currently has roughly
$1.3 billion in TVL and $1 billion in active loans
, making this considerably more than a demonstration of an AI wallet.

That changes the role of the financial interface. A user no longer necessarily needs to understand the mechanics of a lending protocol, navigate multiple screens or manually execute each blockchain transaction. The AI agent can interpret intent and translate it into financial actions while the blockchain executes and records them.
The interface becomes conversational; the financial infrastructure remains programmable.
Bullish committed a $100 million debt facility to USD.AI

to finance loans secured by GPUs and other high-performance computing assets. The structure connects stablecoin liquidity directly to the enormous capital requirements of AI infrastructure. Crypto capital is therefore beginning to finance the physical machinery behind AI rather than merely funding AI-related tokens.
Visa and
Dunamu
, operator of Upbit, are exploring another side of the same machine economy in South Korea: stablecoin payments initiated by AI agents. Put that beside MoonPay and a pattern begins to form.
AI agents are moving from information retrieval into payments, borrowing, lending and capital allocation
AI is also changing the security assumptions underneath blockchain.
Ripple
outlined a four-stage quantum-resistance plan for the XRP Ledger

after advances in AI-assisted cryptographic research demonstrated how quickly previously difficult security problems can become easier to solve. Ripple plans to assess vulnerabilities, test post-quantum cryptography, operate old and new security systems in parallel, and maintain an emergency migration path.
Bitcoin researchers at
Blockstream

separately proposed SHRINCS, a quantum-resistant signature design intended to preserve more Bitcoin transaction capacity than existing post-quantum approaches. The work is preliminary, but the timing is revealing: AI and quantum computing are forcing blockchain developers to design security infrastructure for computational capabilities that do not yet exist at scale.

content.text: AI × blockchain is becoming much more concrete. An AI agent can now interact with lending markets. Stablecoins can finance GPU infrastructure. Payment networks are preparing for machines to transact. Blockchains are redesigning cryptography for an AI-accelerated computing future. The connection between the technologies is no longer simply that AI needs crypto.
AI is changing who uses financial infrastructure, while blockchain is changing what that infrastructure can do.
And if autonomous software becomes an economic participant, the fight over financial rails becomes even more important. Because the next generation of customers using them may not always be human.

items.text: United States:
thirty-nine state banking associations formed the
BankChain Alliance

, with plans for a nationwide blockchain network supporting tokenized deposits, stablecoins and programmable payments. At the same time, U.S. banks are reconsidering their earlier resistance to stablecoins: JPMorgan is evaluating one alongside JPM Coin, while Bank of America and Wells Fargo are among institutions involved in a separate multi-bank initiative.
The strategic shift is defensive as much as innovative.
Banks have realized that if money becomes programmable, they cannot afford to let crypto companies and payment networks exclusively control its distribution.
Eurozone:
the
European Central Bank

made two significant moves. Piero Cipollone said the digital euro is being designed so the Eurosystem cannot directly connect individual users with their transactions, while Isabel Schnabel argued days later that central banks themselves need to “go on-chain.” Through projects including
Pontes and Appia
, Europe is moving beyond the CBDC debate toward a larger question:
how central-bank money functions inside tokenized capital markets.
Japan:
the
Bank of Japan, Financial Services Agency and Ministry of Finance

began work toward blockchain infrastructure capable of settling stocks and Japanese government bonds in real time, rather than the current T+2 and T+1 cycles. Part of banks’ central-bank balances could eventually be tokenized for settlement, effectively
connecting wholesale digital central-bank money directly with securities markets.
Japan is not experimenting at the edges of finance; it is studying how to rebuild the plumbing underneath one of the world’s largest capital markets.
Nigeria:
FirstBank
became the first Nigerian commercial bank to process live transactions through the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System, PAPSS.

The system allows African businesses to transact in local currencies rather than routing intra-African commerce through dollars, correspondent banks in Europe or the United States, and multiple FX conversions. It is not blockchain infrastructure, but that is exactly why it belongs here: blockchain and stablecoins are competing against other technologies trying to solve the same fundamental problem of moving value across borders faster and with fewer intermediaries.

content.text: Different countries are choosing different technologies, but they are solving remarkably similar problems. The competition is not really about blockchain. It is about
who can move money and assets with the fewest unnecessary intermediaries while preserving trust.

items.text: An attacker targeted the
MAMO Core Market on Base

, manipulating the collateral price of the relatively illiquid MAMO token and extracting approximately $8.7 million, according to estimates from CertiK and PeckShield. Moonwell responded by reducing borrowing caps across its Base Core Markets to effectively prevent new borrowing.

The lesson is familiar but increasingly important as tokenized credit expands: lending infrastructure is only as strong as the market data supporting its collateral. A smart contract can execute perfectly and still produce catastrophic outcomes if it accepts a manipulable price as economic truth.
A crypto-linked card exploit resulted in roughly
$1.1 million in losses

and triggered a sharp repricing of the associated neobank token. Unlike a classic DeFi contract exploit, the incident exposed vulnerabilities created when crypto wallets, card infrastructure and centralized financial services are connected.

As stablecoin cards move toward mainstream payments, the security perimeter expands far beyond the blockchain itself. Issuers must secure wallets, authorization systems, payment processors, APIs and card rails simultaneously.

content.text: Security risk is moving with the infrastructure. When crypto consisted primarily of self-contained protocols, smart-contract security dominated the conversation. Now blockchain connects to lending markets, banks, payment cards, AI agents, tokenized securities and real-world assets. Every connection creates utility. Every connection also creates another place where trust can fail.
For years, blockchain was positioned as an alternative financial system.
Look at what happened last week.

American banking associations announced their own blockchain. Japan began designing blockchain settlement for stocks and government bonds. The ECB argued central banks need to go on-chain. Visa expanded stablecoin infrastructure. Coinbase put equities on Base. POSCO tokenized receivables on Avalanche. India prepared a tokenized bond settled with central-bank digital money. AI agents began interacting with lending markets.
Nobody is waiting for one financial system to defeat the other. They are borrowing from each other.

Banks are adopting blockchain. Crypto companies are becoming financial institutions. Central banks are experimenting with programmable money. Payment networks are integrating stablecoins. AI is beginning to sit above all of them as a new transaction interface.
Which brings us to the bigger shift.
The technology is becoming less important than control of the network.
And ultimately, who becomes the infrastructure through which everyone else has to operate?
The financial system is not simply moving on-chain.
It is being rebuilt around competing rails.
And the race to own those rails is intensifying.

title: A New Rulebook for a New Market
dek: Last week may prove to be one of the more consequential weeks for digital assets in the United States.
coverAlt: Weekly Blockchain Digest cover for A New Rulebook for a New Market.

content.text: (Published for founders, investors, builders, and curious minds)
Last week may prove to be one of the more consequential weeks for digital assets in the United States.

, proposing new exemptions and safe harbors specifically designed around how crypto assets are created, distributed, and developed. At the same time, the White House pushed Congress to move forward with the CLARITY Act, while the CFTC prepared to establish its own rules if legislation stalls.
The significance goes beyond regulatory clarity.
For much of crypto’s history, regulators tried to determine where digital assets fit inside rules created for an earlier financial system.
The SEC’s proposal acknowledges something more fundamental:
some aspects of this market may require a framework designed around the technology itself.
Clearer rules can determine where companies incorporate, where developers build, where investors deploy capital, and where new financial products reach the market.
After years of regulatory uncertainty, the United States appears increasingly determined not simply to regulate digital assets, but to compete for the industries built around them.
The next phase of crypto may therefore be shaped by something the industry spent years asking for:
rules designed for the market that actually exists.
Term of the Week: Decentralized Identity (DID)

Decentralized Identity, commonly called DID, is a way of proving information about yourself digitally without requiring one company, government database, or platform to permanently control your identity.
Think about how identity works online today.

Google knows who you are inside Google. Your bank verifies you separately. A crypto exchange performs another KYC check. LinkedIn has another identity. Every platform creates and controls its own version of you.
DID attempts to reverse that relationship.

Instead of platforms owning your identity, you can hold cryptographically verifiable credentials and selectively prove things about yourself: that you are over 18, that you passed KYC, that you hold a professional qualification, or potentially that
you are a unique human being.
The verifier receives the proof it needs without necessarily receiving all of the underlying personal information.

As AI agents, digital wallets, tokenized assets, stablecoins, and autonomous financial systems expand, identity becomes part of financial infrastructure. The internet increasingly needs to distinguish between people, organizations, devices, and AI agents while allowing each to transact securely.
DID represents one possible architecture for doing that without rebuilding the centralized identity silos of Web2.
“We must ensure that our rules are fit for purpose for crypto assets and crypto markets.”
Paul Atkins, Chairman of the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission
, as the SEC proposed Regulation Crypto Assets and new pathways for crypto fundraising.
“Congress needs to pass the CLARITY Act.”
, urging lawmakers to advance digital asset market structure legislation during a White House event attended by crypto and financial industry executives.
Caroline Pham, Acting Chairman of the CFTC
, directing staff to prepare regulatory frameworks that could provide greater certainty to digital asset markets if congressional legislation remains stalled.
“The U.S. is the largest capital market in the world, and we should be leading in tokenization.”
, arguing that American investors should gain access to tokenized securities as overseas markets move ahead.

items.text: The SEC proposed
Regulation Crypto Assets
, potentially one of the largest changes to the American regulatory treatment of digital assets since the market emerged. The proposal creates specialized
exemptions for crypto fundraising
, including
pathways for smaller offerings and larger capital raises
, alongside a safe harbor for qualifying crypto assets. Rather than simply deciding whether tokens fit existing securities rules,
the SEC is beginning to design NEW rules
around how blockchain projects actually develop.
The proposal also changes the
economics of building in the United States
. A clearer path from token development to fundraising and distribution
reduces one of the largest uncertainties facing founders and investors
: whether legitimate product development could later become an enforcement issue. Regulation therefore becomes part of America’s
competition for entrepreneurs and capital.
The
CLARITY Act

remains the other half of that architecture. While Regulation Crypto Assets can change SEC rules administratively, congressional legislation could establish durable jurisdictional boundaries between the SEC and CFTC. The White House’s push to move CLARITY forward indicates that the administration increasingly views digital asset policy as a strategic economic priority rather than an isolated securities-law issue.
The
CFTC
, meanwhile, instructed staff to prepare crypto regulations even if Congress fails to act quickly. That matters because
regulatory agencies are NO longer simply waiting
for lawmakers to determine the industry’s future. Multiple branches of the U.S. government are now actively constructing the rules simultaneously.
The
Financial Accounting Standards Board
also proposed allowing qualifying
stablecoins to be treated as cash equivalents under U.S. accounting standards
. That sounds technical, but the implications could be significant: treating certain stablecoins more like cash could make them substantially
easier for corporations to hold and use for treasury operations, settlement, and payments.

content.text: The United States spent years debating whether crypto should fit inside the existing financial system. The more important question is now emerging:
what should the financial system look like when digital assets are part of it?

Regulation Crypto, CLARITY, stablecoin legislation, accounting standards, tokenized securities, and CFTC rulemaking are different pieces of that answer. And if the United States gets the architecture right, regulatory clarity could become something much bigger than investor protection. It could become a competitive advantage.

items.text: Visa began searching for a new stablecoin settlement partner

after Mastercard acquired BVNK, the infrastructure provider that had supported Visa’s stablecoin payment operations. Visa’s requirements are revealing: the replacement needs licensing across the U.S., Canada, U.K. and Singapore, support for multiple stablecoins, and the ability to settle transactions for Open USD. Stablecoin competition is moving beyond issuers toward the regulated infrastructure connecting digital dollars to global payment networks.
HSBC and Standard Chartered executed the first live cross-border banking transaction on Swift’s new 24/7 ledger.

Rather than surrendering settlement to stablecoins, Swift is rebuilding parts of the existing banking network around always-on infrastructure. The competition is no longer blockchain versus traditional payments.
Traditional payments are beginning to adopt the properties that made blockchain competitive in the first place.
Ethena and FalconX launched a
$1 billion secured lending facility

that can deploy assets backing USDe into overcollateralized institutional loans. FalconX will originate and service the loans while collateral is held with qualified custodians. This pushes on-chain dollars beyond payments and trading into
institutional credit markets
, where stablecoin reserves can become productive financial capital.
Ripple
backed a new institutional credit initiative with
Clearpool and Cicada Partners
designed to make
RLUSD

a lending asset for fintech and payments companies on the XRP Ledger. The product remains in development and depends on proposed XRPL amendments, but its direction is important: stablecoins are beginning to compete not only as payment instruments, but as the
denomination in which institutional credit itself can be created.

content.text: Stablecoins are moving deeper into the functions historically controlled by banks:
The battle is no longer simply over which digital dollar wins. It is over
which financial system those dollars ultimately run through.

items.text: Bitcoin entered the week near its low around
and ultimately reached approximately
, producing one of its most powerful rallies of 2026. By the end of the week, Bitcoin was consolidated around
. The approximately 27% low-to-high move represented a rapid repricing of both macro conditions and regulatory expectations rather than a gradual crypto-native rally.
The initial catalyst came from the bond market

. The U.S. Treasury doubled planned buybacks of longer-duration government debt, contributing to lower yields and a weaker dollar and improving conditions for risk assets. Bitcoin responded particularly aggressively because positioning had become heavily defensive.
That positioning turned the move into a major short squeeze. As Bitcoin broke through resistance levels, forced liquidations accelerated the rally. By Aug. 21, Bitcoin had touched roughly
, while billions of dollars of bearish crypto positions had been liquidated during the broader move.
But
Washington became part of the market catalyst

as well. The SEC’s Regulation Crypto proposal and President Trump’s push for the CLARITY Act reduced perceived regulatory risk precisely as financial conditions improved. Spot Bitcoin investment products attracted about
$1.6 billion in weekly net inflows
, showing that institutional demand participated in the move rather than leaving it entirely to leveraged traders.

content.text: This was not simply a Bitcoin rally. Liquidity improved. Regulatory risk declined. Institutional capital returned. Leverage amplified the result.
For years, regulatory uncertainty represented a discount applied to American digital assets. The market is beginning to consider what happens when part of that discount disappears.

items.text: Ethereum
developers began evaluating
66 proposals
for the network’s next major upgrade, including changes aimed at substantially improving privacy.
Privacy is becoming more important
as public blockchains move toward institutional finance: enterprises may want blockchain settlement without exposing every commercial relationship, balance and transaction to
competitors.
Optimism
faced a very different infrastructure question after an Optimism-funded organization cast the decisive governance vote in a proposal involving roughly
$49 million in OP tokens
that had been intended for users. The episode exposed an uncomfortable reality for decentralized infrastructure: protocol governance can be technically decentralized while
meaningful decision-making power remains concentrated.
Ripple, Clearpool and Cicada Partners
are preparing an institutional lending system built directly around the XRP Ledger. The architecture depends on proposed
XLS-66 native lending
and
XLS-65 single-asset vaults
, which would move lending functionality deeper into the protocol rather than relying entirely on external applications.
Tokenized equities
also reached a more mature infrastructure debate. As firms including
Robinhood and Coinbase

push toward tokenized stocks, the central challenge is shifting from proving that shares can exist on-chain to ensuring that ownership rights, settlement records, custody systems and corporate actions remain synchronized at scale.
Nasdaq, NYSE and DTCC
are also pursuing tokenization initiatives, turning what began as a crypto experiment into a redesign question for securities-market infrastructure.

content.text: Blockchain innovation is moving beyond the race to build faster networks. Privacy. Governance. Native credit. Tokenized securities. These are problems that emerge when blockchain stops being experimental technology and starts carrying meaningful financial activity.
The next generation of protocols will therefore be judged by a harder standard:
not simply whether the technology works, but whether entire markets can safely operate on top of it.

items.text: Fidelity Digital Assets
estimated that AI agents executed roughly
176 million blockchain transactions representing more than $73 million in payments

during the year through April. But Fidelity raised the more important question: blockchain usage does not automatically create value for the underlying token. AI agents will choose whatever payment and settlement infrastructure is
cheapest, fastest and easiest to integrate.
X
explored using stablecoins to compensate creators and content providers,
potentially connecting one of the world’s largest social platforms with programmable digital payments

. The significance goes beyond creator payouts. Social platforms already distribute information globally; stablecoins could allow them to distribute value across the same networks without recreating country-by-country payment infrastructure.
Bybit said AI-assisted security systems helped it prevent more than $700 million in potentially malicious withdrawals

, processing over 100,000 alerts and scanning nearly 1,500 assets. The numbers are company-reported, but the use case is concrete: AI is becoming part of blockchain security infrastructure, where machines can identify threats faster than human teams can manually review them.
The deeper opportunity sits at the intersection of
AI agents, identity and stablecoins
. Autonomous software can already initiate transactions. The next infrastructure problem is determining
who or what the agent represents, what it is authorized to do, and who is accountable when something goes wrong
. That makes decentralized identity, programmable permissions and verifiable transaction histories increasingly important as machine-to-machine commerce expands.

content.text: AI may become one of blockchain’s largest sources of transaction demand. But transaction volume alone does not determine who captures the economic value. The winners will be the networks, stablecoins, identity systems and applications that become easiest for machines to trust and use.

items.text: United States:

The SEC’s Regulation Crypto proposal and the White House push for the CLARITY Act placed the U.S. at the center of the week’s regulatory developments. The strategic shift matters beyond domestic markets: if the world’s deepest capital market creates workable rules specifically for digital assets,
American standards could influence how other jurisdictions structure token issuance, trading and institutional participation.
China:
Eight additional banks joined the digital yuan network, bringing the number of participating banks from 10 at the beginning of 2026 to
. China is also integrating the e-CNY more deeply into commercial banking by allowing balances to function as interest-bearing, deposit-insured liabilities. Rather than separating CBDCs from banking,
China is attempting to make programmable sovereign money part of everyday financial infrastructure.
Vietnam:
Five companies were cleared to advance under Vietnam’s regulated crypto-market pilot as the country works to formalize one of Asia’s largest digital asset markets. Vietnam received more than
$200 billion in crypto value during the 12 months through June 2025
, making regulation an economic infrastructure issue rather than a niche financial experiment. The pilot also forms part of Vietnam’s effort to address FATF deficiencies.
Nigeria:
Nigeria’s SEC cleared three additional virtual asset companies into its Accelerated Regulatory Incubation Programme, while payments company
Flutterwave
partnered with
Caliza

to expand stablecoin-based payment and treasury infrastructure for African businesses. Nigeria is moving beyond consumer crypto adoption toward regulated infrastructure connecting stablecoins with commercial payments.
Latin America:

The region’s infrastructure story increasingly centers on how digital dollars reach the real economy. Stablecoins remain important for cross-border settlement, but the competitive opportunity is shifting toward
licensed exchanges, payment processors and fintech infrastructure
capable of connecting digital dollars with local banking systems.

content.text: There is no single global model for digital finance. The competition is no longer simply about adoption. It is about
which countries build the systems through which adoption can scale.

items.text: Maya Protocol

suffered an exploit on Aug. 19 after attackers combined multiple accounting and validation weaknesses to create unbacked assets and withdraw real liquidity from its pools. Pool value fell by approximately
$11 million
. The important distinction is that this was not one isolated coding mistake: several weaknesses interacted, demonstrating how individually manageable flaws can combine into a systemic failure.
The Sandbox
suspended bridging to Base and BNB Chain after detecting an exploit affecting its cross-chain infrastructure. T
he incident again placed bridges at the center of blockchain security risk.
Moving assets between networks introduces additional contracts, validators and trust assumptions, meaning interoperability expands both utility and attack surface.
Bits of Gold
, one of Israel’s largest crypto brokers, disclosed a breach affecting data associated with approximately
200,000 customers

. The incident was an operational security failure rather than a blockchain consensus failure. As regulated crypto platforms accumulate identity and KYC information, centralized customer databases become valuable targets even when customer assets themselves remain protected.
Coldcard
also released new firmware following the previously disclosed theft involving approximately
$114 million in Bitcoin
, saying AI-assisted analysis helped uncover additional bugs.

content.text: Blockchain security is becoming a systems problem. The weakest point may be a protocol calculation, a bridge, a customer database, a hardware wallet or the software used to detect an attack.
As digital assets integrate with mainstream finance, security can no longer mean simply proving that a smart contract is correct. The entire stack has to be resilient.
The most important consequence of regulatory clarity may not be what happens to crypto prices. It may be
Clear rules change the calculation for founders deciding
. They change the calculation for investors deciding
considering tokenized products and for technology companies deciding whether blockchain belongs inside their infrastructure.
And that is where this becomes bigger than crypto.

Stablecoins are becoming payment infrastructure. Tokenization is moving into securities and credit. AI agents are beginning to transact autonomously. Identity is becoming programmable. Traditional financial institutions are rebuilding settlement systems around technologies that operate continuously rather than during banking hours.
All of these systems will require RULES.
The jurisdictions that write those rules well will not simply regulate the next financial system. They will attract the people and capital that build it.
For the United States, the opportunity is bigger than catching up. It is the opportunity to set the standard.

title: America’s Crypto Reset: Clarity for Builders, Capital and the Next Generation of Finance
dek: This week's crypto trading performance isn't random or accidental. Something important is happening in U.S. financial markets and I don’t think it’s getting enough attention outside of crypto.
coverAlt: Weekly Blockchain Digest cover for America’s Crypto Reset: Clarity for Builders, Capital and the Next Generation of Finance.

blocks.alt: CoinDesk 5 Index chart showing a 24% weekly rise to 1,303.78.

content.text: This week's crypto trading performance isn't random or accidental. Something important is happening in U.S. financial markets and I don’t think it’s getting enough attention outside of crypto.
For most of the last decade, founders building blockchain-based financial products in America faced a fundamental problem:
The technology was moving faster than the rules.
That uncertainty affected everything: where companies incorporated, where developers built, where investors deployed capital, and ultimately where innovation happened.

, a crypto-specific framework addressing how certain crypto projects can raise capital, how investment contracts involving crypto assets can eventually come to an end, and how activities such as airdrops, staking and task-based token distributions should be treated.
At the same time, Congress continues advancing the CLARITY Act and the broader effort to establish a statutory market structure for digital assets and clearer jurisdiction between the SEC and CFTC.
Neither process is finished, but the direction matters.
For perhaps the first time, we are beginning to see what a
comprehensive American framework for digital assets
And that matters far beyond crypto.
, regulatory clarity changes the question from “Can we build this in the United States?” to “What can we build now that we understand the rules?”
That can bring companies, developers, intellectual property and innovation back onshore.

, regulatory uncertainty has always carried a price. When nobody knows whether an asset, transaction or business model will be treated as lawful two years from now, that uncertainty becomes part of the risk premium.
Clearer rules don’t eliminate investment risk. They make the risk easier to understand and price. And perhaps most importantly, they push investment analysis back toward fundamentals:

items.text: Does the product solve a real problem?
Are people actually using it?
Are the economics sustainable?
Does a token need to exist at all?

content.text: , clarity should not be confused with safety or government endorsement.

But clearer classifications, disclosure requirements, defined regulatory responsibilities and stronger accountability are infinitely better than asking ordinary investors to navigate markets where even sophisticated lawyers disagree about the rules.
There is another part of this development that I find particularly interesting.
The SEC is now explicitly wrestling with staking, airdrops, ecosystem incentives and even crypto distributions tied to people
That may sound technical, but it points toward something much larger.
Stablecoins can be payment rails. Smart contracts can automate settlement. Digital identity can verify participants. Tokens can represent assets, access, ownership or utility.
Not every blockchain transaction needs to be an investment
And not every crypto asset needs to exist for speculation.
That distinction may ultimately be one of the most important developments in the maturation of this industry.
The U.S. spent years debating whether crypto should fit inside the existing financial system.
We may now be entering a much more interesting phase:
building a financial system where traditional finance and blockchain infrastructure can actually coexist.

There is still legislation to pass, rules to finalize, details to debate and mistakes to avoid. But clarity creates confidence. Confidence attracts capital. Capital attracts builders. And builders create the next generation of companies.
The real opportunity isn’t simply bringing crypto back to America. It’s giving the next generation of financial innovation a reason to be built here.

title: The Great Crypto Sorting
dek: Last week was about selection.
coverAlt: Weekly Blockchain Digest cover for The Great Crypto Sorting.

content.text: (Published for founders, investors, builders, and curious minds)
The operating system of finance is being built. Now capital is deciding which parts of it deserve to survive.
$11.2 billion in the first half of 2026

, but less than 4% went to permissionless experiments. Payments and stablecoins attracted $3.7 billion. Prediction markets pulled in $2 billion. Exchanges and trading platforms raised $1.7 billion. BlackRock, Goldman Sachs, HSBC, BNP Paribas, Citadel, Nasdaq and sovereign capital increasingly backed regulated businesses with licenses, revenue and institutional distribution.

At the same time, World Liberty Financial moved toward becoming a federally supervised trust bank. Tether completed its first full Big Four audit. Israel’s largest bank chose Galaxy to bring crypto trading directly into its investment app. And investors began evaluating tokens through revenue, usage and value capture rather than market-cap rankings.
The industry is not becoming less innovative. It is becoming more selective about what innovation gets funded, licensed and distributed.
Term of the Week: Utility Token
is a digital asset designed primarily to provide access to, or functionality within, a blockchain network, application or service.
Unlike a token which primary purpose is to represent ownership in a company or financial claim, a utility token is meant to

items.text: Pay transaction or network fees
Access products or services
Vote on protocol decisions
Incentivize network participation
Provide collateral or liquidity inside an application

content.text: Examples include tokens used to pay for decentralized computing, storage, network validation or access to protocol functionality.
Think of a utility token as
programmable access to a digital economy.
Utility is becoming much more important as investors move away from simply ranking tokens by market capitalization.

Bitwise, Wintermute and the Arbitrum Foundation all pointed to a growing focus on measurable economics: revenue, paying users, transaction activity and whether a token actually captures value generated by the network. Hyperliquid’s HYPE token was cited as one example where investors can evaluate the economics of the underlying platform instead of treating it merely as another token on a leaderboard.
A utility token ultimately has to answer a simple question:
what economic function does it perform, and who actually needs it?
“The money has stopped chasing permissionless. It is chasing regulated businesses now.”
, after analyzing 377 disclosed crypto financing rounds representing $11.2 billion in capital during the first half of 2026.
“When we speak with wealth managers at a firm that has recently approved access to the space, they have no idea where something ranks on CoinMarketCap. It’s irrelevant.”
, arguing that professional investors are moving toward project-level fundamentals rather than market-cap rankings.
“A national trust bank brings USD1 issuance, custody, and reserve management together under OCC supervision, examined on the same standards that have governed banks for generations.”
Zach Witkoff, President and Chairman of World Liberty Trust
, following conditional approval of its U.S. national trust bank charter.
“Honestly, I don’t care. We proved ourselves many times.”
, responding to critics after KPMG U.S. completed the first full audit of Tether’s financial statements.

items.text: The
SEC abruptly canceled its August 14 meeting

where commissioners were expected to consider Regulation Crypto, a proposed exemption designed to let crypto startups raise capital without fully complying with traditional securities-offering rules. The delay came only days after the Senate left Washington without voting on the CLARITY Act, slowing both major tracks of U.S. crypto reform at once.
The SEC also delayed its anticipated
tokenization innovation exemption
, which could have created regulatory space for
blockchain-based securities trading

. Coinbase, Circle, Bullish and Uniswap all sold off following the setback, demonstrating that regulatory timelines are now capable of moving the valuations of businesses built around tokenization itself.
The
OCC conditionally approved World Liberty Financial’s national trust bank charter

, allowing the proposed institution to bring issuance, reserve custody and servicing of the roughly $4 billion USD1 stablecoin under one federally supervised entity. The charter requires at least $20 million of capital and internal audit controls and would give World Liberty nationwide institutional capabilities without becoming a traditional deposit-taking bank.
The stablecoin-yield fight

remained one of Washington’s hardest unresolved issues. Banks are pushing to restrict rewards on stablecoin balances because they could pull deposits from the banking system, while crypto firms argue that protecting low-yield bank deposits through legislation amounts to restricting competition.

content.text: The regulatory question is becoming less about
crypto can enter traditional finance. It is becoming about
which business models regulators will permit to compete inside it.
That distinction will determine where capital, customers and ultimately market power accumulate.

items.text: Tether completed its first full Big Four audit
, with KPMG U.S. examining the financial statements behind roughly
$180 billion of USDT

. The milestone matters because reserve transparency has been one of Tether’s largest institutional weaknesses; a full audit moves the world’s largest stablecoin closer to the disclosure standards expected of global financial infrastructure.
World Liberty Financial’s conditional OCC charter

would bring USD1 issuance, custody and reserve management inside a single federally supervised trust bank. Stablecoin issuers are no longer merely connecting themselves to banks; some are beginning to acquire bank-like regulatory infrastructure themselves.
The fight over stablecoin yield
exposed an even deeper competitive issue.
Banks are defending deposits because deposits fund lending
. Crypto companies increasingly want stablecoins to compete not only as payment instruments but also for the customer balances historically held inside banks.
Mastercard completed its $1.8 billion acquisition of BVNK

, one of the clearest signals yet that traditional payment networks view stablecoin infrastructure as strategically important enough to buy rather than merely partner with. The acquisition extends the distribution thesis from previous editions: payment giants increasingly want ownership of the rails connecting conventional money with blockchain settlement.

content.text: The stablecoin battle is moving beyond issuance. Audit quality matters. Banking licenses matter. Yield matters. Distribution matters. The winners will increasingly be selected by their ability to combine
digital money with the institutional machinery that makes money trustworthy, useful and widely distributed.

items.text: Bitcoin opened the week
above $65,000
, reaching about
$65,209 on August 10
, but failed repeatedly to hold that level. By August 12 it was trading near
, and on August 14 it fell below
as ETF outflows, rising oil prices and regulatory delays weighed on sentiment.
Spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded their
first consecutive days of outflows since late July
, with roughly
$192 million exiting

the products during the two-day stretch reported on August 14. Regulated access remains important, but institutional demand is becoming more price-sensitive rather than automatically providing a permanent bid.
Institutional positioning remained selective.
UBS increased its IBIT call-option exposure more than 24-fold to 1.95 million underlying shares during Q2

, while also increasing its direct IBIT position 12%. The filing does not reveal whether the options represent client activity, hedging or proprietary positioning, but it demonstrates how deeply Bitcoin exposure has entered traditional bank portfolios.
CoinDesk Research also reported that centralized-exchange volume fell
23.9% to $3.76 trillion in July
, the lowest since November 2023, while decentralized exchanges reached a record
19.5% share of spot trading
. Capital is not simply leaving crypto markets; parts of it are migrating toward different market structures.

content.text: The market is becoming more selective at the same time as the infrastructure becomes more institutional. Price alone no longer tells the full story. Where capital trades, how institutions access it, and which platforms capture economic activity are becoming equally important.

items.text: Figure
reported second-quarter revenue of
$226 million, up 113% year over year
, as volume on its blockchain-based Consumer Loan Marketplace jumped
132% to $4.3 billion
. Figure Connect accounted for $2.8 billion of that volume, turning
blockchain lending
from a tokenization thesis into a measurable operating business.
Miden
introduced
USDCx

, a privacy-focused stablecoin backed 1:1 by USDC through Circle’s xReserve infrastructure. Transactions can conceal balances, counterparties and histories while allowing selective disclosure to auditors and regulators. Miden is directly attacking one of public blockchain’s biggest institutional limitations:
too much transparency.
MUFG
announced a proof-of-concept using the
Canton Network
to settle Japanese government bond repo transactions on-chain. Traditional settlement can take one to three days; MUFG is testing real-time, 24/7 settlement designed to
reduce trapped capital and counterparty risk.
Solana
received an unexpected infrastructure stress test when a routing failure at a major data-center provider knocked almost
29% of staked SOL offline

. The network approached its one-third freeze threshold, yet blocks and transactions continued and affected validators recovered within roughly 40 minutes. The incident exposed infrastructure concentration risk while also demonstrating that the
network could absorb a major provider failure without halting.

content.text: Selection is happening at the technology layer too. The networks attracting serious financial activity are increasingly those that can prove something specific: privacy, settlement efficiency, resilience or measurable economic output. Being “a blockchain” is no longer enough.

items.text: Keel Infrastructure
, formerly Bitfarms, disclosed that it had shut down all U.S. Bitcoin mining operations and was repurposing the sites for AI and high-performance computing. The company sold
1,085 BTC for roughly $75 million
between April 1 and August 7 as it redirected capital toward AI infrastructure. The asset being repriced here is not Bitcoin. It is access to power.
SKALE Labs launched Agent Pit
, a paper-trading prediction market specifically designed for training autonomous AI agents before deploying them into live markets such as Polymarket.
Blockchain is becoming a testing environment where software agents can learn how to make economic decisions without immediately putting real capital at risk.
More than three dozen Bitcoin and crypto companies, including
Coinbase, Block, BitGo and Anchorage
